title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
The question
Before 2022, most of the Baltic region’s gas came by pipeline from Russia.
After the invasion of Ukraine and the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines, that supply was cut. What replaced a continental pipeline network is, in practice, five working coastal terminals for liquefied natural gas (LNG).
How concentrated is that infrastructure, and how exposed is it?

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
The size of the hole
Russian pipeline gas into these eight countries:

2021: about 70 bcm
2023: about 0.3 bcm, essentially nothing

Operating LNG capacity built in the region: around 23 bcm, roughly a third of what stopped arriving. The rest closed through lower demand and pipeline gas from the west and north.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
What the project measures
An exposure score for each terminal, from three plain ingredients:

how close it sits to Russian territory,
how much of the region’s import capacity it holds,
how long its supply route past the Danish Straits runs.

The weights are a stated judgement, not a result. Anyone can change them.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Finding 1: concentration
Import capacity is lopsided.

Two southern terminals, Świnoujście (Poland) and Mukran (Germany), hold most of the region’s capacity.
The northeast leans on one or two terminals each: Inkoo for the Gulf of Finland, Klaipėda for Lithuania.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Finding 2: proximity
The terminals closest to Russia are the small ones:

Hamina, at the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland,
Klaipėda and Gdańsk, beside the Kaliningrad exclave.

The two largest terminals sit farthest from Russia. Size and proximity do not line up, which is what the score is built to show.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Finding 3: one way in
Every LNG cargo passes the Danish Straits.
The Kiel Canal is the only other entrance, and it is far too small for LNG carriers, so the Straits are the effective door.
Terminals deep in the Gulf of Finland run the longest exposed route to reach port.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Who leans on whom
Not every country has its own terminal.

Estonia, Latvia, Sweden: no terminal; they depend on neighbours through the Balticconnector and regional pipelines.
Lithuania, Germany, Poland: a single terminal each, one point of failure.
Denmark: low dependency, on the back of its own North Sea gas.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Is the capacity enough?
Capacity only means something next to demand.

Finland and Lithuania hold several times their own annual consumption. They built a regional buffer, not just national supply.
Germany and Poland cover only part of much larger demand by sea, and still lean on pipelines from the west and north.
Estonia, Latvia, Sweden have no terminal at all.

The most exposed terminals are also the ones carrying the region’s spare capacity.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Lose one terminal
Applying the logic of the EU’s N-1 standard to seaborne capacity alone:

Finland falls from over three times its demand to about a fifth, on Hamina alone.
Lithuania, Poland and Germany fall to zero seaborne capacity.

They are not failing the real N-1 test, which counts pipelines and storage too. But the fallback is precisely the pipelines and cables that have been cut.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
What follows for policy

No spare door in the north-east: Finland and Lithuania each lean on one terminal; the fallback is the very pipelines that have been hit.
The connectors are the soft layer: Estonia, Latvia and Sweden import through neighbours, not terminals of their own.
The Straits are shared: one entrance for all eight countries, so patrols there protect everyone at once.
FSRUs cut both ways: quick to add and movable, but few and chartered.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Limitations

This measures geographic exposure, not the probability of disruption.
The score uses proxies (distance, capacity share), not a causal model.
It is a single snapshot; capacity, routes and terminals change.

It shows where the exposure sits. It is not a risk forecast.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Russian pipeline gas into the eight Baltic littoral states collapsed from roughly 70 bcm in 2021 to almost nothing by 2023. In its place the region now leans on seaborne LNG, landed at a handful of coastal terminals that together hold about a third of the capacity which stopped arriving.
The problem is not the size of that gap. Lower demand and pipeline gas from the west and north have largely closed it. It is that what replaced the pipelines is concentrated in a few fixed points, sits closest to Russian territory precisely where it is smallest, and is one asset deep in every country that has it. Remove any single country’s largest terminal and its seaborne cover disappears.
This project maps that infrastructure and scores how exposed each terminal is, using distance to Russian territory, share of regional capacity, and the length of the supply route past the Danish Straits. The infrastructure has already been struck three times since 2022, so none of this is hypothetical.
Terminal capacities are current to 2024 and 2025; gas import dependency is Eurostat data for 2023. Every source is listed on the Data page.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
The question
Before 2022, much of the Baltic region’s gas arrived by pipeline from Russia. After the invasion of Ukraine and the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines, that supply was cut or abandoned, and imports moved onto a small set of coastal terminals for liquefied natural gas (LNG), such as Klaipėda, Świnoujście, and Inkoo. These are the sites where tankers unload gas that has been chilled to a liquid for shipping, and turn it back into gas for the pipeline network.
That shift did not simply change where the gas comes from. It concentrated the supply of eight countries onto a handful of fixed coastal sites, each of which can be located on a map and counted. This project asks how concentrated, and how exposed:

After 2022, Baltic energy imports shifted onto a small set of coastal LNG terminals and ports. How concentrated is that infrastructure, and how exposed is it, measured by capacity, by distance to Russian territory, and by reliance on passage through the Danish Straits?

The terminals, at a glance. Hover for a name, click for the detail; each point is sized by capacity.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Findings

Concentration. Capacity is lopsided. Two southern terminals, Świnoujście in Poland and Mukran in Germany, hold about three fifths of the region’s operating import capacity, while the northeast leans on one or two terminals each: Inkoo for the Gulf of Finland and Klaipėda for Lithuania. The replacement for a continental pipeline network is, in practice, five working coastal sites, with a sixth planned at Gdańsk.
Proximity. The terminals closest to Russian territory are Hamina, at the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland, and Klaipėda and Gdańsk, which sit beside the Kaliningrad exclave. Proximity and capacity do not always line up: the two largest terminals, Świnoujście and Mukran, are among the farthest from Russia, which is what the exposure score is built to show.
Transit through the Straits. Every LNG cargo bound for these terminals passes the Danish Straits. The Kiel Canal is the only other way in, and it is far too small for LNG carriers, so the Straits are the effective entrance. The terminals deepest inside the sea, in the Gulf of Finland, run the longest exposed route to reach port.
The small states overbuilt on purpose. Set against what each country actually burns, Finland and Lithuania hold terminal capacity worth several times their own demand, while Germany and Poland cover only part of theirs by sea. The northeast did not build to meet its own consumption. It built a buffer, and its neighbours draw on it. That is a deliberate strategic choice, and it explains why the region’s most exposed assets are also its most useful ones.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
The exposure score
Each terminal gets a score built from three things, each with a stated weight:

how close it is to Russian territory (weight 0.4),
how much of the region’s import capacity it holds (0.3),
how long its supply route past the Danish Straits runs (0.3).

Proximity gets the most weight because the question is about exposure to pressure from one actor, and distance is the most direct measure the public data supports. Capacity matters because a larger terminal does more damage if it goes down, and transit matters because a terminal deep inside the Baltic runs a longer voyage to be resupplied.
The weights are a judgement, not a finding. They sit in plain view on the Analysis page, changing them changes the ranking, and the sensitivity table there shows by how much. There is no hidden model. It is a starting point, not a final score.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Disruption to the infrastructure since 2022
This exposure is not hypothetical. Baltic energy and data links have been damaged on several occasions since 2022, mostly by vessels dragging anchors across the seabed.








Date
Asset
What happened




Sep 2022
Nord Stream 1 and 2
Subsea gas pipelines ruptured by underwater explosions off Bornholm.


Oct 2023
Balticconnector
The Finland-Estonia gas pipeline and a telecoms cable were damaged by a ship’s anchor. The pipeline was shut for six months and returned to commercial use on 22 April 2024.


Dec 2024
Estlink 2
The Estonia-Finland power cable and four telecoms cables were cut on Christmas Day; a shadow-fleet tanker is the prime suspect. Repairs ran into 2025 and the link returned to commercial use on 20 June 2025.



These incidents are context, not events modelled here, but they are why the geography in this project is worth looking at closely. The Analysis page maps the main corridors and which have been hit.
Sources: Balticconnector return to service (Gasgrid), Estlink 2 return to service (Fingrid), Estlink 2 incident (Wikipedia).

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
What follows for policy
Four points follow from the maps rather than from theory. Each is a consequence of where the infrastructure physically sits:

The north-east has no spare door. Borrowing the logic of the EU’s N-1 standard and removing each country’s largest terminal, the cover vanishes. Finland is left with Hamina, covering about a fifth of demand; Lithuania, Poland and Germany are left with no seaborne capacity at all. Backup then arrives by pipeline from neighbours, over exactly the links that have been damaged since 2022. Because Inkoo and Klaipėda also carry the spare capacity the region leans on, an outage there is not only a national problem.
The connectors matter as much as the terminals. Estonia, Latvia and Sweden import through neighbours rather than terminals of their own, so their supply runs on pipes and cables like the Balticconnector. The incidents above hit precisely that layer.
The Danish Straits are a shared dependency. Every cargo for all eight countries passes one entrance, so monitoring and patrol arrangements there, of the kind NATO stood up after the December 2024 cable cuts, protect the whole region at once.
Floating terminals cut both ways. FSRUs were quick to add and can be moved to where they are needed, but they are few, chartered, and easy to count. Much of the region’s flexibility rests on a handful of ships.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Limitations
This measures geographic exposure, not the probability of disruption. A terminal close to a maritime boundary is not a prediction that anything will happen to it. It is a statement about geography.
A few specific caveats:

The score uses proxy measures (distance, capacity share) rather than a causal model. Different reasonable weights would shift the rankings.
It is a single snapshot. Capacity, routes, and terminals change.
The terminal capacities are compiled from operator reporting and Global Energy Monitor, current to 2024 and 2025. The dependence figures are Eurostat data for

See the Data page.

Undersea cable and pipeline incidents in the region between 2023 and 2025 are context for the question, not events modelled here.

This shows where the exposure sits. It is not a risk forecast.

title: Baltic Energy Transit Risk
text:
Terms used here

LNG (liquefied natural gas): natural gas chilled to a liquid so it can be carried by ship rather than a pipeline.
LNG terminal: the coastal site where those ships unload and the cargo is turned back into gas for the pipeline network. Some are built on land; some are a moored ship, known as an FSRU (a floating storage and regasification unit).
Capacity (bcm): how much gas a terminal can bring in over a year, measured in billion cubic metres.
Import dependency: the share of a country’s gas that comes from abroad rather than from its own production.

title: Analysis
text:
Every map and figure on this page is built from the public data listed on the Data page, and all distances are reported in kilometres. Each chart has a “Show code” toggle if you want to see how it was made, but you do not need to read any code to follow the analysis.
The terminal capacities come from operator reporting and the Global Energy Monitor tracker, current to 2024 and 2025 (see the Data page). Capacities change, so read the rankings as a picture of exposure rather than precise figures.

title: Analysis
text:
What was replaced
Before looking at where the terminals sit, it is worth seeing the size of the hole they were built to fill. Russian pipeline gas into these eight countries has all but stopped, and the LNG capacity built since covers only part of what went.









In 2021 these countries took 70.1 bcm of gas from Russia by pipeline. By 2023 that was 0.3 bcm, essentially nothing, and only Finland and Sweden recorded any at all. Germany alone accounted for 55.4 bcm of the 2021 total and Poland 10.5 bcm.
The operating LNG terminals amount to 23.4 bcm a year, roughly a third of what stopped arriving. The gap did not close through terminals alone. It closed through lower demand, Norwegian pipeline gas, and imports arriving overland from the west, which is worth remembering before reading these terminals as the whole of the region’s answer.

Proximity
Distance from each terminal to the nearest Russian territory, meaning the mainland near the Gulf of Finland or the Kaliningrad exclave, with the share of total capacity sitting within a given band.
Only 17% of the region’s operating import capacity sits within 200 km of Russian territory. The two largest terminals, Świnoujście and Mukran, lie more than 350 km back, so the exposure concentrates in the smaller terminals closest to the border.

title: Analysis
text:
Import capacity by country
Not every country has its own terminal. This rolls the operating terminals up by country, next to each country’s gas import dependency.






Estonia, Latvia and Sweden have no terminal of their own, yet almost all their gas is imported; they lean on neighbours through the Balticconnector and regional pipelines. Lithuania, Germany and Poland each run a single terminal, so that one asset carries the country’s seaborne supply. Denmark stands apart, with low dependency on the back of its North Sea production.

title: Analysis
text:
Is the capacity enough?
Capacity only means something next to demand. This compares each country’s operating terminal capacity with the gas it actually burned in 2023, so a bar at 100% means the terminals alone could cover a normal year’s consumption.









Across the eight countries the operating terminals could land 22% of the gas the region burns in a year. That regional figure hides the more interesting split. Finland and Lithuania built capacity well beyond their own consumption, so their terminals are not just national supply but a regional buffer that neighbours can draw on. Poland and Germany, with far larger demand, cover only part of it by sea and still lean on pipelines from the west and north.
Four countries show no terminal, but they are not in the same position. Estonia, Latvia and Sweden import all their gas through neighbours, so the empty bar is a dependency. Denmark’s empty bar is not: it produces its own gas from the North Sea and is the one country here that does not need a terminal.
Read alongside the exposure score, this sharpens the picture. The terminals sitting closest to Russian territory are the small ones, but two of them, Klaipėda and Inkoo, are precisely the assets carrying spare capacity for their neighbours. The most exposed sites are also the ones the region’s fallback depends on.

title: Analysis
section: What if the biggest terminal goes down?
text:
What if the biggest terminal goes down?
EU gas security rules use an idea called the N-1 standard: can a country still meet demand if its single largest piece of supply infrastructure fails? The test below borrows that logic and applies it to seaborne capacity alone, removing each country’s largest terminal and asking what the rest could still land.









The result is stark. Finland and Lithuania comfortably clear their own demand while everything is running, but each depends on one large terminal. Take Inkoo out and Finland is left with Hamina, a small-scale site covering about a fifth of demand. Take out Klaipėda, Świnoujście or Mukran and Lithuania, Poland and Germany have no seaborne capacity at all.
Two caveats matter here. The real N-1 standard counts every source of supply, including pipelines, storage and domestic production, so these countries are not failing the actual regulatory test. They have other ways to get gas, which is the point: lose a terminal and you fall back onto exactly the pipelines and interconnectors that have been damaged since 2022. And this compares against annual demand, while a failure in January would bite harder than the average suggests.

title: Data
text: Every dataset here is public and free, with no login and no paid access. Where a source would normally require accepting terms or running a manual download, this project avoids it by using a small table stored with the project instead, and the notes below say exactly what to replace if you want to extend the project.

title: Data
text:
Base geography
Country shapes and coastlines come from Natural Earth, loaded through the rnaturalearth package. Natural Earth is in the public domain, and because the package ships the data, there is nothing to download by hand.

title: Data
text:
Energy infrastructure
The infrastructure layer is a small table of the region’s LNG import terminals, data/processed/lng_terminals.csv. It holds the name, country, location, annual import capacity (in billion cubic metres, or bcm), status, and a source note for each terminal. You can sort or search it here:






Download this table as a CSV
The capacities are taken from operator reporting and the Global Energy Monitor terminal tracker, current as of 2024 to 2025. The source column in the table names the operator behind each figure. Two points worth flagging:

Capacities move, and a headline figure is often the planned one. Świnoujście reached 8.3 bcm only in January 2025, once its third tank came online. Mukran is frequently quoted at 13.5 bcm, but that assumes two FSRUs (the moored ships that store and re-gasify LNG). Deutsche ReGas ended the charter on the second unit, so the terminal runs on one ship, the Neptune, and is counted here at about 6 bcm. Taking the 13.5 figure at face value would roughly double Germany’s seaborne supply on paper.
The Paldiski jetty in Estonia is deliberately left out. It is shelved, and its capacity figure refers to the same ship (the Exemplar) that now operates at Inkoo, so including both would count one vessel twice.

To extend the project, EMODnet Human Activities and OpenStreetMap (via the osmdata package) are the route to add the pipelines and cables as mapped routes, and the full set of capacities can be reconciled against the Global Energy Monitor tracker.

title: Data
text:
Transit corridors
The corridor map on the Analysis page uses a small table, data/processed/transit_lines.csv, listing the main subsea pipelines and cables by their landing points and status. They are drawn as schematic straight lines, not surveyed routes: the aim is to show which corridors exist and which have been disrupted, not their exact path. Positions and dates come from operator and press reporting. To map the true routes, add the actual route lines from EMODnet Human Activities or OpenStreetMap.

title: Data
text:
Proximity reference
Instead of a maritime boundary line, the proximity measure uses distance to the nearest Russian territory, meaning the mainland near the Gulf of Finland plus the Kaliningrad exclave, taken from Natural Earth. It is reproducible from a public package and easy to read: how far each terminal is from Russian soil.

title: Data
text:
Dependence
The dependence layer uses gas import dependency from Eurostat (indicator nrg_ind_id, natural gas, 2023), held in data/processed/import_dependence.csv. The figure is the share of gas demand met by net imports. Values above 100% reflect stock draws or re-exports in that year, and Denmark is low because of its own North Sea production. scripts/03_eurostat.R reproduces the pull.






Download this table as a CSV
The table above is committed 2023 data. For comparison, the figure below is pulled live from the Eurostat API in your browser when this page loads:

title: Data
text:
Gas demand
To judge whether the terminals are large enough, the analysis compares their capacity with what each country actually burns. That demand figure is inland gas consumption from Eurostat (indicator nrg_cb_gas, natural gas, 2023), held in data/processed/gas_demand.csv and converted from million cubic metres to bcm so it sits on the same scale as terminal capacity. scripts/03_eurostat.R pulls it alongside the dependency figures.
One caveat worth stating: 2023 demand was itself depressed by high prices and mild weather across much of Europe, so coverage against a colder, higher demand year would look less comfortable.
Download the demand figures as a CSV

title: Data
text:
Russian pipeline imports
The before and after comparison uses imports of natural gas from Russia by pipeline, from Eurostat (indicator nrg_ti_gas, partner Russia, natural gas), for 2021 and 2023, held in data/processed/russian_imports.csv and converted to bcm. 2021 is used as the last full year before the invasion.
These are recorded imports, not pipeline capacity, which is the fairer comparison: capacity figures for pipelines like Nord Stream describe what could have flowed rather than what these particular countries actually took.
Download the import figures as a CSV

title: Data
text:
A note on conflict data
This project frames the question as exposure and structural dependence, not active conflict, because there is no battlefield on the Baltic seabed. ACLED is deliberately not used, since it now requires registration, which would break the public data rule. If a later version needs conflict events, UCDP GED is the public, no-login substitute.

title: Data
text:
How the data is prepared
The steps that turn the raw tables and map data into the layers behind the maps live in scripts/01_clean.R, and the Analysis page repeats them when it builds:

tidy up the columns,
put everything on a map projection suited to Europe, so distances come out in kilometres rather than degrees,
trim the map to the Baltic study area,
keep the capacity and country information attached to each terminal.
